query: Where is Django's QuerySet class defined?
expected_answer_summary: django.db.models.query.QuerySet, defined at db/models/query.py:374.
notes: Complete miss -- db/models/query.py's QuerySet class never retrieved. Every one of the top 6 results is a real variable literally named 'where' (SQL WHERE-clause-building locals in constraint/index code), because the query's own interrogative 'Where is...' collided with that extremely common Django ORM variable name. Same no-stopword-filtering mechanism as SQLAlchemy's 'a'/'defined' collisions, now triggered by the question word itself.

query: Where is Django's base Model class defined?
expected_answer_summary: django.db.models.base.Model, defined at db/models/base.py:508, using the ModelBase metaclass.
notes: Complete miss -- db/models/base.py's Model class never retrieved.

query: Where is the CSRF protection middleware implemented?
expected_answer_summary: django.middleware.csrf.CsrfViewMiddleware, defined at middleware/csrf.py:165.
notes: Success -- django.middleware.csrf module and django.core.checks.security.csrf._csrf_middleware both retrieved directly. This is the deliberate positive-control counterpart to Flask/FastAPI's CSRF negative queries (Django genuinely does implement CSRF protection, unlike those two): confirms Veyra's exact/substring name-match tier works well when a real, distinctively-named entity exists, and that the CSRF negative-query failures elsewhere are a genuine false-premise-detection gap, not just Veyra being generally bad at anything CSRF-related.

query: What does django.contrib.auth.authenticate() actually call to check a user's credentials?
expected_answer_summary: authenticate() (contrib/auth/__init__.py:124) loops over the configured authentication backends and calls each one's authenticate() method (e.g. ModelBackend.authenticate, backends.py:65) until one succeeds.
notes: Success -- contrib.auth.__init__.authenticate (and its async twin aauthenticate) both retrieved directly.

query: What is Django's default Manager class actually built from?
expected_answer_summary: Manager (manager.py:176) is not written directly against QuerySet by inheritance in the usual sense -- it's dynamically constructed by BaseManager.from_queryset(QuerySet), which copies QuerySet's public methods onto a generated Manager subclass.
notes: Complete file-level miss, but a topically-adjacent one: retrieved several real 'default_manager' variables/attributes (Options.default_manager, serializer default_manager handling) which are genuinely part of the same Manager subsystem, just not the Manager class definition (manager.py) itself. Closer to the right neighborhood than most other misses.

query: How does an incoming WSGI request get dispatched to the correct Django view function, end to end?
expected_answer_summary: WSGIHandler (core/handlers/wsgi.py:113) receives the raw WSGI call and builds a WSGIRequest; get_response() (core/handlers/base.py:138) runs it through the middleware chain; _get_response() (base.py:176) resolves the request's path via the URL resolver (URLResolver.resolve, urls/resolvers.py:670) and calls the resulting view callback.
notes: Complete miss, and a particularly clean demonstration of the stopword-collision root cause: this benchmark's own query phrasing ('...end to end?') put the word 'end' in the query, and Django's codebase has 'end'/'end_index' as an extremely common variable name (string/slice indexing) across many unrelated files -- all 6 top results share only that one incidental token with the query. None of WSGIHandler, get_response, or the URL resolver chain appear anywhere.

query: How does Django apply configured middleware to every request?
expected_answer_summary: load_middleware() (base.py:27) builds a nested chain of middleware callables around the core view-dispatch function, storing it as self._middleware_chain; get_response() (base.py:138) invokes that chain (line 142) on every request, so each configured middleware wraps the next one in order.
notes: Complete miss -- BaseHandler.load_middleware/get_response never retrieved for the middleware-application architecture question.

query: What happens when CsrfViewMiddleware detects a POST request without a valid CSRF token?
expected_answer_summary: CsrfViewMiddleware (middleware/csrf.py:165) rejects the request with a 403 Forbidden response instead of letting it reach the view function.
notes: CsrfViewMiddleware._check_token.request_csrf_token retrieved directly (2nd result) -- genuinely relevant, though the specific process_view rejection path isn't confirmed in the reviewed portion.

query: What does authenticate() return if the given credentials don't match any configured authentication backend?
expected_answer_summary: authenticate() (contrib/auth/__init__.py:124) returns None when no configured backend can authenticate the credentials.
notes: Success -- same authenticate()/aauthenticate() hit as django-04, correctly the same underlying function both times.

query: If a Django app's migrations aren't being applied in the order I expect, where should I look?
expected_answer_summary: MigrationExecutor (db/migrations/executor.py:10) is responsible for resolving the dependency graph between migrations and determining the order they run in -- that's where ordering issues trace back to.
notes: Complete miss, another clean stopword-collision case: this query's first-person 'where I expect' put the single letter 'I' in the token stream, colliding with the extremely common loop-counter variable name 'i' across totally unrelated files (SQL compiler internals, template parsing, HTML testing utilities). MigrationExecutor never appears.

query: Where would I investigate if a custom Manager isn't exposing a custom QuerySet method I defined?
expected_answer_summary: Manager's methods come from BaseManager.from_queryset() (manager.py:176 shows the default Manager built this way from QuerySet) -- a custom QuerySet's methods only reach a Manager if the custom manager was itself built via Manager.from_queryset(MyQuerySet); that's the first place to check.
notes: Complete miss -- same Manager/from_queryset gap as django-05.

query: How does registering a model in the admin (admin.site.register) connect it to Django's admin URLs?
expected_answer_summary: admin.site.register() associates a model with a ModelAdmin instance (options.py:686); AdminSite.get_urls() (sites.py:258) iterates all registered models and builds URL patterns pointing at each ModelAdmin's views, which get included into the project's normal URL resolution.
notes: contrib.admin.decorators.register (the @admin.register decorator, a real and relevant entry point) is retrieved directly, but AdminSite.get_urls -- the specific URL-wiring method this cross-file query asks about -- is absent from what was reviewed.

query: Where does Django implement its own production-grade HTTP/2 server?
expected_answer_summary: Django has no production HTTP/2 server implementation in this repository. It ships only a development server (runserver) and expects production deployments to use a separate WSGI/ASGI server (e.g. gunicorn, uvicorn) in front of it.
notes: Negative query (no built-in production HTTP/2 server). Retrieved LiveServerThreadTest.test_server_class's 'server'/'server_class' variables -- Django's real, but test-only, HTTP server used for browser-based test fixtures. A careless reading could mistake this for evidence of production server functionality, though the surrounding test-class context makes it a weaker false-premise risk than sqla-13/fastapi-13.

query: Where does Django implement a built-in GraphQL API layer?
expected_answer_summary: Django has no built-in GraphQL support in this repository. GraphQL support is provided by third-party packages (e.g. graphene-django), not Django core.
notes: Negative query (no built-in GraphQL). Retrieved 'graph' variables from the migrations dependency-graph system (test_autodetector, test_executor) -- pure substring/token collision on 'graph', with enough surrounding migration-specific context that this is unlikely to actually mislead a reader, unlike django-13/sqla-13/fastapi-13. Still no confidence signal, but the lowest false-premise risk among the negative queries reviewed.

query: Where is the FastAPI application class defined, and what does it extend?

query: Which class represents a single registered API route (path + handler + metadata)?
expected_answer_summary: fastapi.routing.APIRoute, defined at routing.py:1126, subclassing starlette.routing.Route.
notes: PHASE D RESULT: still a complete miss on the actual entity (fastapi.routing.APIRoute is rank 60 of 4529, score 15.47, nowhere near retrieval). The raw file-level metric shows 'hit'/recall=1.0/precision=1.0 because the one entity that did clear the threshold, APIRouter.__init__ (30.04), happens to live in the same file (routing.py) -- but APIRouter and APIRoute are two different classes; this is name-similarity coincidence, not a real match. Flagged explicitly since it's a concrete illustration of the benchmark spec's own warning that file-level recall can look better than entity-level correctness actually is (same caveat already documented for flask-06).

query: Where is the Depends() function used for dependency injection defined?
expected_answer_summary: fastapi.param_functions.Depends, defined at param_functions.py:2283; it constructs and returns a fastapi.params.Depends instance (params.py:746).
notes: PHASE D RESULT: a real regression, root-caused rather than left unexplained. fastapi.param_functions.Depends is not matched by search()'s exact_name tier for this query (that tier requires the full query string to equal an entity's name verbatim -- 'Where is the Depends() function...' never does, for any query phrased as a sentence; this is pre-existing search() behavior Phase D did not touch). The baseline's TRUE verdict therefore came from Depends() ranking first under raw cosine similarity, not from an exact-name match despite the original note's label. Under BM25, Depends() drops to rank 19 of 1778 (score 29.58 -- again just above the confidence threshold, but outside the top_k=10 window), overtaken by FastAPI/APIRouter HTTP-verb decorator methods (get/post/options/...) whose docstrings apparently share more BM25-weighted terms with this query than Depends()'s own short docstring does. A concrete, verified instance of the same top_k=10-window issue found in flask-08/fastapi-01, not a new failure mode.

query: What does FastAPI.add_api_route actually call to register the route?
expected_answer_summary: FastAPI.add_api_route() (applications.py:1165) forwards all its arguments to self.router.add_api_route() (APIRouter.add_api_route, routing.py:2889), which actually constructs the APIRoute and appends it to the router.
notes: PHASE D RESULT: unchanged. query: What calls get_dependant() to build a route's dependency graph?
expected_answer_summary: get_dependant() (dependencies/utils.py:271) is called when an APIRoute is constructed (routing.py:1126), building the Dependant object that solve_dependencies() later walks at request time.

query: How does FastAPI resolve a path operation function's dependencies (Depends(...) parameters) at request time?
expected_answer_summary: Each route's Depends() parameters are analyzed once at registration time into a Dependant tree by get_dependant() (dependencies/utils.py:271); on every request, the handler built by get_request_handler() (routing.py:375) calls solve_dependencies() (dependencies/utils.py:586), which recursively resolves and invokes each dependency callable.

None of get_dependant/solve_dependencies/get_request_handler retrieved; dominated by the same HTTP-verb decorator methods (FastAPI.get/options/..., APIRouter.get/options/...) seen across several other fastapi queries, which apparently share heavy vocabulary overlap with many of this benchmark's questions.

query: How does FastAPI generate its OpenAPI schema?
expected_answer_summary: get_openapi() (openapi/utils.py:585) walks the app's registered routes and, for each one, calls get_openapi_path() (openapi/utils.py:311) to build that path's operation entry, assembling the full OpenAPI document.

FastAPI.openapi (34.79), the property that calls get_openapi() internally, is retrieved and is a closer near-miss than baseline's noise, but is not itself the answer.

query: What happens when a request body fails Pydantic validation?

notes: PHASE D RESULT: unchanged from Phase B. Still a complete miss on RequestValidationError/request_validation_exception_handler, still correctly reports insufficient_evidence=True rather than showing wrong entities.

query: What response does FastAPI send back when a path operation raises HTTPException?
expected_answer_summary: http_exception_handler() (exception_handlers.py:11) is FastAPI's default handler for HTTPException (exceptions.py:17); it returns a response using the exception's status_code and detail as the JSON body.
notes: PHASE D RESULT: unchanged. Neither HTTPException (rank 32, score 20.46) nor http_exception_handler (rank 747, score 6.67) clears the threshold; dominated by the same HTTP-verb decorator methods as fastapi-06.

query: Where would I look to debug why a FastAPI endpoint's OpenAPI docs are showing the wrong response schema?
expected_answer_summary: The OpenAPI schema per path comes from get_openapi_path() (openapi/utils.py:311), which reads the response_model and related fields stored on each APIRoute (routing.py:1126) -- a wrong schema traces back to how those fields were set when the route was registered (APIRouter.add_api_route, routing.py:2889).

The specific baseline noise (CI/tooling scripts with a coincidental 'debug' field) is gone, replaced by FastAPI.__init__ and the same HTTP-verb decorator methods -- still wrong, but no longer the tooling-script false-relevance pattern baseline flagged.

query: If a dependency function isn't being re-run per request when it should be, where should I look?
expected_answer_summary: solve_dependencies() (dependencies/utils.py:586) is where per-request dependency resolution and its use_cache-based caching behavior live; unexpected re-use vs. re-execution of a dependency traces back to this function's cache-key logic.
notes: PHASE D RESULT: unchanged. solve_dependencies() is still not retrieved; dominated by APIRouter/FastAPI constructors and unrelated security-scheme classes.

query: How does a security scheme like OAuth2PasswordBearer connect to a path operation's dependencies?
expected_answer_summary: OAuth2PasswordBearer (security/oauth2.py:433) is a callable SecurityBase subclass; when passed to Depends(), get_dependant() (dependencies/utils.py:271) special-cases SecurityBase dependencies so they're both resolved like any other dependency AND recorded as a security scheme for the OpenAPI schema.

OAuth2PasswordBearer.__init__ (47.98) and the OAuth2PasswordBearer class itself (45.01) are both now retrieved near the top -- the primary entity the question names. SecurityBase and get_dependant (the mechanism that actually connects a security scheme to a path operation's dependencies) are still absent, so the 'how does it connect' half of the question isn't answered -- scored PARTIAL, not TRUE, since only the named class, not the connecting mechanism, is present.

query: Where does FastAPI implement its own SQL query builder or ORM?

query: Where does FastAPI implement built-in rate limiting for endpoints?

query: Where is the Flask application class defined?
expected_answer_summary: flask.app.Flask, defined at app.py:110, subclasses flask.sansio.app.App (sansio/app.py:59).

Under BM25, both target entities score below the recalibrated 29.0 threshold (flask.app.Flask: rank 3 of 1250, score 21.40; flask.sansio.app.App: score 22.25) -- verified by direct re-query. insufficient_evidence is now True (0 entities), where the old cosine score used to let at least one of these two classes clear its (much weaker) threshold. This is the direct, documented cost of BM25's saturating term-frequency + per-type length normalization scoring these two large, general-purpose classes lower relative to this query's short, generic token set ('flask', 'application', 'class', 'defined') than raw cosine did. Recorded honestly rather than omitted -- Phase D measurably helped several other queries (see flask-05/07/08/11, fastapi-12) but this is a real, symmetric cost on this one.

query: Which class implements Flask's default (cookie-based) session storage?

query: Where is the Request class that Flask uses for incoming HTTP requests defined?

query: What does the @app.route decorator actually call to register a URL rule?
expected_answer_summary: route() (Scaffold, scaffold.py:344) is a decorator factory that calls self.add_url_rule(rule, endpoint, f, **options); on a Flask app the method resolution order means App.add_url_rule (sansio/app.py:605) is what actually runs, and it registers a werkzeug Rule on self.url_map.
notes: PHASE D RESULT: unchanged. Scaffold.add_url_rule (38.15) and Scaffold.route (36.03) both retrieved and well-ranked; correctly supports the route()->add_url_rule() chain, same as baseline.

query: What class does Flask's Blueprint inherit from?
expected_answer_summary: flask.blueprints.Blueprint subclasses flask.sansio.blueprints.Blueprint (imported as SansioBlueprint), which itself subclasses Scaffold.

The target entity (src.flask.sansio.blueprints.Blueprint) is now present, real, and reasonably ranked -- rank 3 of the raw BM25 results, score 18.66 -- compared to being effectively absent/buried under noise pre-Phase-D. However, 18.66 remains well below the 29.0 confidence threshold (calibrated on real relevant/irrelevant separation, not to pass this query), so retrieve_context still reports insufficient_evidence=True and the query still scores FALSE. Honest summary: the mechanism Phase D targeted did improve here, but not enough to cross the deliberately-conservative confidence bar.

query: How does Flask dispatch an incoming WSGI request to the correct view function, end to end?
expected_answer_summary: wsgi_app() is the WSGI entry point; it pushes a request context and calls full_dispatch_request(), which runs preprocess_request(), then dispatch_request() (which resolves the matched URL rule's endpoint and calls the view function), then finalize_request() which calls process_response().
notes: PHASE D RESULT: unchanged. Of the 5 ground-truth methods (wsgi_app, full_dispatch_request, preprocess_request, dispatch_request, finalize_request), only Flask.dispatch_request (31.79) clears the threshold; the other 4 are still absent. Same shallow-retrieval shape as baseline.

query: How does Flask sign and verify session cookies to prevent tampering?
expected_answer_summary: SecureCookieSessionInterface builds an itsdangerous URLSafeTimedSerializer from app.secret_key via get_signing_serializer(); Flask itself only wires this up -- the actual signing/verification algorithm lives in the itsdangerous dependency, not in the Flask repository.
notes: PHASE D RESULT, checked specifically per instruction #9. Same pattern as flask-05: the target entity (src.flask.sessions.SecureCookieSessionInterface) is now present and reasonably ranked -- rank 6 of the raw BM25 results, score 18.52 -- versus being buried/absent before. Still below the 29.0 threshold, so insufficient_evidence=True and the query still scores FALSE. Both flask-05 and flask-07 land in the same place: a real, measured ranking improvement that the confidence threshold (deliberately calibrated against negative-query leakage, not against these two queries) does not yet convert into a correct answer.

query: What happens when app.run() is called with debug=True?
expected_answer_summary: Flask.run() (app.py:633) sets debug on app.config if passed, then delegates to werkzeug.serving.run_simple with use_debugger/use_reloader enabled when debug is true, which enables the interactive debugger and the auto-reloader.
notes: PHASE D RESULT. This was the flagship reproduction case for Phase D's root-cause investigation (see tests/retrieval/test_retrieval_search.py's test_a_large_relevant_method_outranks_a_tiny_entity_sharing_one_token, modeled directly on this query). Direct verification: Flask.run() moved from being completely buried under 1-token test variables named 'called'/'debug' (baseline) to rank 13 of 1121 real candidates, score 20.38 -- a genuine, large improvement in relative ranking. But retrieve_context's semantic tier is called with top_k=10, and rank 13 doesn't make that cut, so Flask.run() still never reaches the caller and the query still scores FALSE. This is a distinct, newly-identified limitation from the confidence-threshold one above: Phase D fixed the *scoring* pathology this case was built to catch, but a fixed top_k=10 window on top of a corrected score is its own separate bottleneck, not something Phase D's scope (document-length bias in the score itself) covers. Flagging for a later phase rather than widening top_k here without validation.

query: What does Flask do when a request comes in for a URL that doesn't match any registered rule?
expected_answer_summary: The werkzeug URL adapter's match() raises a routing exception (typically NotFound); Flask's raise_routing_exception (sansio/app.py:563) re-raises it so the app's normal error-handling / 404 response path takes over.
notes: PHASE D RESULT: unchanged. sansio/app.py is retrieved via the App class (45.92) but the specific answering method, App.raise_routing_exception, is still absent from the top 10. Right file, wrong entity, same as baseline.

query: If a Flask view function raises an unhandled exception, where should I look to see how Flask decides what response to send back?
expected_answer_summary: full_dispatch_request() catches exceptions from dispatch_request() and routes them to handle_user_exception() (app.py:868), which looks for a registered errorhandler; if nothing handles it (or it's not an HTTPException) it falls through to handle_exception() (app.py:900), which builds the generic 500 response.
notes: PHASE D RESULT: unchanged. Flask.handle_user_exception and Flask.handle_exception are still absent from the retrieved entities; the Flask class itself is retrieved (52.39) but not the specific error-handling methods the question actually needs.

query: Where would I investigate if Flask's test_client() isn't preserving cookies across multiple requests in a test?
expected_answer_summary: FlaskClient (testing.py:109) is Flask's test client; cookie-jar behavior across requests comes from the werkzeug.test.Client base class it extends, with EnvironBuilder (testing.py:27) constructing each request's environ.
notes: PHASE D RESULT: a genuine fix. src.flask.testing.FlaskClient -- the primary entity the question needs ("where would I investigate if test_client() isn't preserving cookies") -- is now retrieved at rank 1, score 41.26, clear of the noise (unrelated 'test_client' local variables) that buried it at baseline. EnvironBuilder (the secondary supporting class named in ground truth) is not retrieved, but scored TRUE under the same standard already applied to flask-02 (correct primary answering entity present and well-ranked, even though not every named ground-truth symbol is).

query: How does registering a Blueprint on a Flask app connect the blueprint's routes to the app's URL map?
expected_answer_summary: App.register_blueprint() (sansio/app.py:570) calls Blueprint.register() (sansio/blueprints.py:273), which replays the blueprint's deferred route registrations against a BlueprintSetupState; BlueprintSetupState.add_url_rule() (sansio/blueprints.py:87) prefixes the blueprint's rules and calls back into the app's own add_url_rule, which is what actually adds them to app.url_map.

query: Where is Flask's built-in ORM or database layer implemented?

query: Where is the Session class defined?

Confirms and sharpens the length-bias finding: a generic phrasing choice ('...class defined?') collided with an incidental naming convention in this specific codebase.

query: Where is the Engine class defined?

query: Where is the Table class defined?

expected_answer_summary: create_engine() returns an Engine (engine/base.py:2893); the Engine itself does not execute statements directly -- a Connection (engine/base.py:90), obtained from the Engine, is what executes SQL.

query: What does Session.add() do to an object before it's actually written to the database?
